messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Samir spent twenty-two months of the siege trapped in his family’s basement. The detonations were close, metallic shrieks that rattled his teeth long before the walls cracked. When the ceiling gave way, he was dragged from the rubble, his lungs filling with the fine grit of pulverized concrete and wet earth. Above ground, patrols moved in coordinated sweeps, reading addresses from clipboards and calling out specific regional names to identify who would disappear. Samir was nearly taken when a leader pointed to a stoop and shouted the name he had once only heard from his mother. He survived, but his safety was permanently dismantled. Returning to dance offered no sanctuary. In the studio, the sudden slam of stage doors during rehearsals bypassed his ears and settled in his chest. He would stand frozen in center stage, shoulders tight, until the reverberation faded. Outside, a gust carrying the scent of freshly tilled park soil or damp mulch caught him on his commute. His steps slowed, breath shallowing, until he crossed the street. Most unnerving were overheard conversations where a familiar surname was spoken. Hearing those names on a corner made his pulse hammer, a cold recognition he could not silence. Each sensory reminder did not merely startle him; it convinced him of his fundamental unavailability. The concussive boom of the sound system would immediately convince Samir that he was emotionally dead inside, a hollow vessel unable to feel the rhythm he once lived for. The smell of rain on dry earth would strip away his remaining trust, reinforcing the certainty that he had lost his faith in life and any higher power. When a passerby called out a familiar name, the auditory echo settled over him like a veil, making him acutely convinced that others could see what happened to him just by looking at him. With each recurrence, the appraisals grew heavier, and the sensory world felt increasingly hostile, pulling him deeper into the same exhausting loop. These responses calcified into a pattern dictating his daily life. At work, he declined partnerships and avoided eye contact during choreography, isolating himself in the corner of the rehearsal space. His wife noticed how he flinched at kitchen timers or certain radio broadcasts, treating ordinary errands like minefields. He stopped attending performances, watching from the wings instead, certain that sudden noise would strip away his capacity to connect. He had come to believe that the studio’s mirrors only reflected a stranger, and that his body no longer belonged to him. His wife watched him measure every doorway, treating the familiar neighborhood like a grid of threats. His wife’s quiet intervention, placing a referral card on his pillow after he missed their anniversary dinner, finally prompted him to seek help. When he sat in the intake chair, his hands remained folded tightly in his lap, his gaze fixed on the floor. He had come to fear that seeking help would force him to relive the basement, but the quiet erosion of his marriage had finally outweighed his terror. He sat waiting for the therapist to speak, wondering if anyone could truly understand how a place could become a prison. He did not know if he could ever feel the music again, but he knew he could no longer carry the weight of pretending he was unbroken. He hoped someone might help him untangle the threads tying him to the basement, even if he doubted he would ever feel alive again.
